In the conjoint experiment, respondents evaluated twenty-six hypothetical constitutions, which were randomly assigned twelve different enumerated rights and institutions (attributes). For example, some constitutions were described as enshrining the freedom of expression and/or fiscal decentralization, while others were not. These attributes were selected to reflect what many constitutional scholars consider to be core individual and social rights and institutional checks and balances. We estimate the average marginal component effect (AMCE) of these twelve attributes, or the average change in constitutional ratings in the presence versus absence of a provision. ¹⁶ Earlier studies, such as Chilton and Versteeg, have considered support for individual provisions such as gender equality. ¹⁷ But to our knowledge, this is the first experimental test that seeks to estimate preferences about constitutional content spanning multiple (twelve) provisions systematically.

excerpts: Reflective Equilibrium - Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy Reflective equilibrium is a formal expression of standard methodological practice in moral and political philosophy.
(See Rawls 1971, e.g., 19–21, for a famous application of reflective equilibrium, and Rechnitzer 2022 for a reconstruction of Thomson 2008 in terms of reflective equilibrium.)
One important kind of argument is the thought experiment.

For instance, in relation to the principle of utility, one might consider utilitarian sheriffs, utility monsters, experience machines, trolley problems, and repugnant conclusions, among countless others.
We are also to consider arguments _against_ principles. The arguments show the strengths and weaknesses of the principles under consideration (Daniels 1996: 82).
A wide reflective equilibrium is achieved where the deliberator has brought judgments and principles into agreement having reflected on a wide range of considerations.

Second, our initial judgments are _revisable._ If you encounter a principle that seems to fit many of your most important judgments, or even that does not fit them but has appeal nonetheless, you are free to change judgments that disagree with that principle.

In moral and political philosophy, the judgments used in reflective equilibrium are usually these Rawlsian considered judgments. Intuitions are frequently used interchangeably with considered judgments in the critical literature on reflective equilibrium. But intuitions as typically described have characteristics that are not generally true of considered judgments, especially non-inferentiality (Brun 2014; Greenspan 2015; Cath 2016: 228–229). This entry will therefore focus on considered judgments rather than intuitions.

Second, our initial judgments are _revisable._ If you encounter a principle that seems to fit many of your most important judgments, or even that does not fit them but has appeal nonetheless, you are free to change judgments that disagree with that principle. Perhaps a principle even ranges over terrain on which you had no prior judgments (e.g., moral dimensions of generative AI), in which case you can make new judgments that agree or disagree with it, as you see fit. Everything is up for grabs.
Reflective equilibrium, at least on its classic construal, arises where judgments are brought together with their representation in principles.
Theories play a dual role as agglomerations of the principles and priority rules that are the outputs of reflective equilibrium, and as sources of argument for selecting those principles.

Third, we are to consider not just a very wide range of principles, but _a wide range of_ _arguments_ for them. Ideally we should consider all such arguments (Rawls 1971: 49). We are also to consider arguments _against_ principles. The arguments show the strengths and weaknesses of the principles under consideration (Daniels 1996: 82). One important kind of argument is the thought experiment. For instance, in relation to the principle of utility, one might consider utilitarian sheriffs, utility monsters, experience machines, trolley problems, and repugnant conclusions, among countless others. A “directed reflective equilibrium” offers a sequencing for consideration of such cases (Slavny et al. 2021). Note that such arguments may not only support one principle over another, but generate new principles, such as variant forms of utilitarianism—and there will be new arguments for and against these variants, which generate their own variants, and so on.

In short, the method of reflective equilibrium is the mutual adjustment of principles and judgments in the light of relevant argument and theory. Reflective equilibrium is the dominant method in moral and political philosophy (McPherson 2015: 652; Anderson 2015; de Maagt 2017: 444). Its advocates suggest that “it is the only rational game in town for the moral theorist” or “the only defensible method” (DePaul 1993: 6; Scanlon 2003: 149; see also Freeman 2007: 35–36; Floyd 2017: 377–378). Though often endorsed, it is far more frequently used. Wherever a philosopher presents principles, motivated by arguments and examples, they are likely to be using the method. They are adjusting their principles—and with luck, their readers’—to the judgments suggested by the arguments and examples. Alternatively they might “bite the bullet” by adjusting initially discordant judgments to accommodate otherwise appealing principles.

excerpts: Forecasting is a fundamental part of planning in the modern world. A forecaster is one who, after observing a series of historical facts, undertakes to guess some related future event. His materials are the available data about the past; facts about some specified phenomenon in several past epochs. Using the traditional statistical techniques of fore— casting, he considers the facts and arrives at some opinion as to the future course of this phenomenon. The forecaster is not a prophet but he is a believer in trends and he has some faith in the continuity of nature. Short—term forecasts of events that may occur next week or next month are usually accurate enough to be useful. But the uncertainties multiply rapidly when long-range forecasts are required and many of the planning decisions must of neces— sity be based on a series of intuitive judgments. Intuition and judgment permeate all analysis, not only as to which hypotheses should be tested or what facts are relevant but also in supplementing a model of a process when the quanti— tative mathematical model is known to be inadequate. It is inevitable that as questions to be answered get broader and more complex, intuition and judgment must supplement quanti-— tative analysis to an increasing extent.

Potential Applications The judgment of experts may be called on in any planning operation in which it is necessary to choose among several alternative courses of action and no theory has been developed which would evaluate the consequences of the proposed courses of action with one course singled out as the preferred alterna— tive by traditional maximization procedures. We use an expert because he has at his disposal a large store of background knowledge and a cultivated sensitivity to its relevance which permeates his intuitive insight. We need a consensus of experts because individual experts will disagree and we are unwilling to rely on the judgment of a single specialist. There are many examples of the use of expert judgment for prediction. One example is provided by the field of medical diagnostics. Another is in the use of the advice of an expert investment counselor. There are some indications that the Delphi process would be useful as a business forecasting tool. Market forecasts are often judgment forecasts and the group response arrived at by the Delphi procedure might prove to be more accurate than reliance on any one individual. Several areas of industrial forecasting ranging from financial planning to sales prediction may be fertile areas. Some of the management decisions made in the promotion and distribution of products and in product pricing problems might be enriched by information obtained from the Delphi procedure.

excerpts: Reflective Equilibrium - Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy Reflective equilibrium is a formal expression of standard methodological practice in moral and political philosophy.
(See Rawls 1971, e.g., 19–21, for a famous application of reflective equilibrium, and Rechnitzer 2022 for a reconstruction of Thomson 2008 in terms of reflective equilibrium.)
One important kind of argument is the thought experiment.

For instance, in relation to the principle of utility, one might consider utilitarian sheriffs, utility monsters, experience machines, trolley problems, and repugnant conclusions, among countless others.
We are also to consider arguments _against_ principles. The arguments show the strengths and weaknesses of the principles under consideration (Daniels 1996: 82).
A wide reflective equilibrium is achieved where the deliberator has brought judgments and principles into agreement having reflected on a wide range of considerations.

Second, our initial judgments are _revisable._ If you encounter a principle that seems to fit many of your most important judgments, or even that does not fit them but has appeal nonetheless, you are free to change judgments that disagree with that principle.

In moral and political philosophy, the judgments used in reflective equilibrium are usually these Rawlsian considered judgments. Intuitions are frequently used interchangeably with considered judgments in the critical literature on reflective equilibrium. But intuitions as typically described have characteristics that are not generally true of considered judgments, especially non-inferentiality (Brun 2014; Greenspan 2015; Cath 2016: 228–229). This entry will therefore focus on considered judgments rather than intuitions.

Second, our initial judgments are _revisable._ If you encounter a principle that seems to fit many of your most important judgments, or even that does not fit them but has appeal nonetheless, you are free to change judgments that disagree with that principle. Perhaps a principle even ranges over terrain on which you had no prior judgments (e.g., moral dimensions of generative AI), in which case you can make new judgments that agree or disagree with it, as you see fit. Everything is up for grabs.
Reflective equilibrium, at least on its classic construal, arises where judgments are brought together with their representation in principles.
Theories play a dual role as agglomerations of the principles and priority rules that are the outputs of reflective equilibrium, and as sources of argument for selecting those principles.

Third, we are to consider not just a very wide range of principles, but _a wide range of_ _arguments_ for them. Ideally we should consider all such arguments (Rawls 1971: 49). We are also to consider arguments _against_ principles. The arguments show the strengths and weaknesses of the principles under consideration (Daniels 1996: 82). One important kind of argument is the thought experiment. For instance, in relation to the principle of utility, one might consider utilitarian sheriffs, utility monsters, experience machines, trolley problems, and repugnant conclusions, among countless others. A “directed reflective equilibrium” offers a sequencing for consideration of such cases (Slavny et al. 2021). Note that such arguments may not only support one principle over another, but generate new principles, such as variant forms of utilitarianism—and there will be new arguments for and against these variants, which generate their own variants, and so on.

In short, the method of reflective equilibrium is the mutual adjustment of principles and judgments in the light of relevant argument and theory. Reflective equilibrium is the dominant method in moral and political philosophy (McPherson 2015: 652; Anderson 2015; de Maagt 2017: 444). Its advocates suggest that “it is the only rational game in town for the moral theorist” or “the only defensible method” (DePaul 1993: 6; Scanlon 2003: 149; see also Freeman 2007: 35–36; Floyd 2017: 377–378). Though often endorsed, it is far more frequently used. Wherever a philosopher presents principles, motivated by arguments and examples, they are likely to be using the method. They are adjusting their principles—and with luck, their readers’—to the judgments suggested by the arguments and examples. Alternatively they might “bite the bullet” by adjusting initially discordant judgments to accommodate otherwise appealing principles.

This entry first addresses the judgments that are the starting point for reflective equilibrium, examining various interpretations of them found in the literature. It then explores the principles and theories that take us from merely having judgments to reaching reflective equilibrium. Finally, it considers some of the main objections to the method. But the uncertainties multiply rapidly when long-range forecasts are required and many of the planning decisions must of neces— sity be based on a series of intuitive judgments. Intuition and judgment permeate all analysis, not only as to which hypotheses should be tested or what facts are relevant but also in supplementing a model of a process when the quanti— tative mathematical model is known to be inadequate. It is inevitable that as questions to be answered get broader and more complex, intuition and judgment must supplement quanti-— tative analysis to an increasing extent. The Delphi process is representative of an important class of techniques that need to be developed for further applications to decision making situations. It involves one of the methodological aspects of modern practice in operations research, namely the reliance on judgment of experts. For many years experts have been used in brainstorming sessions and round-table discussion groups with the object of achieving a group opinion, a group solution to a problem or a group estimate of some unknown numerical quantity. The tradi- tional discussion approach was often beset by psychological factors such as the presence of a dominant, persuasive personality, the tendency to want to meet the approval of the group and the unwillingness to change an opinion which had been publicly expressed. Helmer and Rescher [1] point out that the Delphi Technique "eliminates committee activity altogether, thus further reduc— ing the influence of certain psychological factors, such as specious persuasion, the unwillingness to abandon publicly expressed opinions, and the bandwagon effect of majority opinion. This technique replaces direct debate by a care— fully designed program of sequential individual interrogations (best conducted by questionnaires) interspersed with informa— tion and opinion feedback derived by computed consensus from the earlier parts of the program. Sone of the questions directed to the respondents may, for instance, inquire into the reasons for previously expressed opinions and a collection of such reasons may then be presented to each respondent in the group, together with an invitation to reconsider and possibly revise his earlier estimates. Both the inquiry into the reasons and subsequent feedback of the reasons adduced by others may serve to stimulate the experts into taking into due account considerations they might through ... a case might consist of specialists in sociology, demography and population growth. This question was imbedded in one part of the panel on Population Control in Helmer's 'Long—Range Forecasting Study" [2]. I have simplified it for use as an illustrative example. The procedure will be described by pursuing the response to this question through the successive questionnaires. In the first questionnaire, all respondents would be asked to record their estimate of the world population in 2000. Each respondent would also be asked to assign a number 1, 2, 3, or 4 as a relative rating, using 1 for the relatively most competent. This score would constitute a self—appraisal. A respondent would be expected to look at all of the questions in the set and assess his relative competency on each one. The information from these responses which would furnish feedback data for the second interrogation would be the median and the interquartile range (i.e., the middle 50 percent of the responses). In the second round, respondents would be asked to reconsider their estimate and revise it if they desired. They would also be asked to give the reasons for the estimate and state what factors were considered in obtaining the answer. They may also be asked to describe the rationale that led them to a revision of their original estimate. Some of the reasons given for population estimates at the low end of the scale were (a) rapid increase in use and effectiveness of birth control measures, (b) increased economic prosperity, (c) progress in welfare and education in the developing nations and (d) attrition due to war and disease Among the reasons for high estimates were (a) medical advances resulting in lower death rates, (b) insufficient acceptance of birth control measures, (c) development of centralized world government providing efficient distribution of food, shelter and services and (d) advances in agriculture. Participants indicated that they projected birth rates and death rates and net growth rates in arriving at the population estimates. In the third questionnaire, the median and interquartile range of the previous round would be given along with a sum- mary of reasons for high and low population estimates. Participants would be asked to give a critique of the reasons offered by members of the group and to specify which arguments were found to be unconvincing and why. Responses to the third round included estimates that the death rate would drop from 19 per 1000 to a figure between 10 and 17 per 1000 and that birth rates would decline from 36 per 1000 to a figure between 15 and 26 per 1000. In the fourth round the median and interquartile range of the previous round would again be used as numerical feed— back. The counter~arguments against reasons for high and low estimates would be summarized. Majority and minority opinions on the projection of death rates and birth rates would be described and respondents then asked to reconsider the pros and cons presented and give a final, possibly revised, estimate of the world population in the year 2000. Each respondent would also be given an opportunity to revise his own relative competence rating. The median of these final responses would then be taken to represent the group response on the required answer. Some Modifications of the Procedure The objective of a given inquiry and the special problems associated with the area of expertise being tapped might suggest a number of modifications or refinements. In the illustrative example of obtaining an estimate of world population in 2000, the respondents could be asked to suggest subsidiary questions whose answers would be helpful in formulating the estimate. Respondents might ask some of the following questions: What is the world population at the present time? What was the rate of increase of population during the last 50 years? What is ‘the expected length of life at age 1 at the present time in the U.S.? What percent of the 1900 world population were 18 years old or less? What percent were 65 or older? Answers to these subsidiary questions could be solicited from the group and fed back to the participants. It would also be possible to use a member of the control team administering the experiment or an outside specialist as a "resource analyst,” and answers to the subsidiary questions could be researched and passed to the participants as supplementary information along with the citation of the reference source. This procedure could become cumbersome if the number of questions under consideration were sizable. In the course of a few years, it should be possible to equip each expert with a console through which he could feed his responses into a computer. The computer would process them, compute some measures of the group response, possibly add relevant information from an existing data bank and feed the results back to each respondent. At the Rand Corporation, small Delphi experiments are being conducted that use a number of personal electric typewriter consoles connected through an on-line time-sharing computer system. How Delphi Method has been Used A small experiment called "Twenty Questions" [3] was con— ducted at Rand in 1964 using staff members as participants. The ‘purpose was to get some insight into the methodology of the Delphi process, and the questions submitted to participants were World Almanac type questions for which numerical answers were available. The experiment was designed to determine to what extent initially divergent opinions of a group of persons would converge if successive questioning were re-enforced by a feedback process in which respondents were given information from other members of the group. The set of respondents was divided into two groups, a primary group and a control group. The primary group completed four questionnaires with feedback information. The control group participated in two rounds only, with no feedback at all. The results of the experiment indicated that a sharper consensus was obtained by the primary group, that the total range of the responses was reduced on successive rounds but the accuracy of the group estimate was no greater with the primary group than with the control if we compare them on the response to the second round. It is necessary to state what criterion was used to measure accuracy. In this case, it was the sum of the absolute values of the logarithm of x/T, where x is the group median response and T is the true answer. It was evident that a reconsideration of the questions fostered convergence in both the primary and the control groups. | An experiment in which the Delphi technique was applied was reported by Dalkey and Helmer [4]. The results of the experiment were released for open publication in 1962 but the experiment itself was conducted about ten years earlier. In this application, expert opinion was applied to the dual problem of the selection of an optimal industrial target system and the estimation of the number of A-bombs required to reduce the munitions output by a prescribed amount. Seven experts participated, responding to five questionnaires submitted at approximately weekly intervals. The first questionnaire was followed by an interview in which each respondent was asked to reproduce the reasoning by which he arrived at an estimate of the number of bombs and to show the component breakdown by industries. The third also was followed by an interview for the clarification of ambiguities. The choices of target systems were quite distinct, the only common feature being the inclusion of the steel industry in each. The numerical quantity being estimated showed considerable convergence. The ratio between the largest and smallest response was about 100 to 1 on the initial round but had dropped to about 3 to 1 on the final round. A first application of the Delphi technique to long—range forecasting was made in 1964 [2] in an investigation in which several panels of experts were asked to'make contingency fore— casts of the state of the world twenty—five to fifty years hence. Six groups of experts were selected, one for each area of inquiry. Each panel answered four sequential questionnaires spaced approximately two months apart. The six areas covered were scientific breakthroughs, population growth, automation, space progress, war prevention and future weapon systems. The six groups of respondents made judgments on more than 200 \-10— predictive items during the course of the experiment. The substantive outcome of the investigation cannot be summarized here. A few thought—provoking examples of some of the pre— dictions that were articulated by the experts have been selected from pages 45-46 of the Gordon and Helmer report [2]. (1) The implication that the water—covered portions of the earth may become important enough to warrant national territorial claims; (2) the possibility that continued, developments in automation will result in serious social upheavals and the almost complete acceptance of the necessity of regulative legislation; (3) the strong likelihood of the emergence of weapons of a nonkilling, nonproperty—destroying nature, covert perhaps, attacking on the psychological or biological level; (4) the eventual abundance of resources of energy, food, and raw materials, but also the possibility that a continuing inequitable world distribution of these assets to the increasing world population may furnish a persisting stimulant to warfare. A study, entitled Innovation in Education, was carried out at the Institute of Government and Public Affairs at UCLA under the sponsorship of the Charles F. Kettering Foundation during 1966\. The report was published by authors Adelson, Alkin, Carey and Helmer [5]. This study was an attempt by a multi-— disciplinary group to generate some perspectives on possible changes in american education. The Delphi technique was included as part of the investigations because the researchers conjectured that it might be useful as a planning aid for those who make educational policy. Respondents examined and made —ll- judgments on a list of nearly one hundred proposed educational innovations covering a wide range of educational activities. Proposed innovations covered Curriculum, Teaching Methods, School Administration, Student Participation, Staff Utilization, Adult Retraining, Automated Education, etc. In the preparation of the final round, each of the proposed items was assigned to a gross cost category. If a respondent thought the cost category assignment for a given innovation was inappropriate, he was expected to state the reason for his position. However, the principal task for the respondents in the final question— naire was to allocate a fictitious 5 year budget of ten billion dollars among the proposed innovations. The authors state that the participants found it difficult to make the required choices even though they were well informed in the field and were used to making decisions. The results of the study indicated that the Delphi technique may be potentially useful in educational planning. Robert M. Campbell[6] used the Delphi technique in a study in which business and economic indices were forecast. He conducted a controlled experiment using students in two graduate seminars in business forecasting. Each seminar was divided at random into two equal groups. All four groups were asked to make forecasts of 16 economic series for the first quarter of 1966. The participants were informed of the experi— ment about a month in advance and were given some guidance on accumulating information which would develop their expertise without revealing the actual series to be forecast. One group \-12— in each seminar used the traditional methods of making business forecasts and the other used the Delphi process. The traditional method allowed participants to interact freely with others in ‘the group for the purpose of obtaining information relative to the forecasts. The Delphi experimental group gave individual responses to a series of four questionnaires over a period of six weeks. The group participants who used the Delphi process made more accurate forecasts than the group uSing the traditional business forecasting technique. A study was conducted within TRW, Inc. [7] in an attempt to predict the operating environment of the company twenty years hence. The method used was to ask each member of a panel of 27 technologists to list events of a technical nature that were likely to occur within the next 20 years. Participants were from all working groups in the company and each man was expected to Suggest events that might have substantial impact on potential product lines of his group. The lists of technological break— throughs were collected by mail. These were compiled and the completed document was returned to each panelist with the sug— gestion that he should edit freely in his own area of expertise. The TRW probe of the future resulted in a list of about 400 events with predicted dates of occurrence representing the judgment of responsible experts in several areas of research. The results constitute an information source for planners throughout the corporation. ~13— Potential Applications The judgment of experts may be called on in any planning operation in which it is necessary to choose among several alternative courses of action and no theory has been developed which would evaluate the consequences of the proposed courses of action with one course singled out as the preferred alterna— tive by traditional maximization procedures. We use an expert because he has at his disposal a large store of background knowledge and a cultivated sensitivity to its relevance which permeates his intuitive insight. We need a consensus of experts because individual experts will disagree and we are unwilling to rely on the judgment of a single specialist. There are many examples of the use of expert judgment for prediction. One example is provided by the field of medical diagnostics. Another is in the use of the advice of an expert investment counselor. There are some indications that the Delphi process would be useful as a business forecasting tool. Market forecasts are often judgment forecasts and the group response arrived at by the Delphi procedure might prove to be more accurate than reliance on any one individual. Several areas of industrial forecasting ranging from financial planning to sales prediction may be fertile areas. Some of the management decisions made in the promotion and distribution of products and in product pricing problems might be enriched by information obtained from the Delphi procedure. —14— Often there are variables used as inputs to models for which no adequate measure exists. An example might be a policy decision ‘model in which measures of social and cultural conditions in some of the developing nations are needed. There are no historical records available. The obvious recourse is the efficient use of the intuition and judgment of a group of persons who are keen observers and have lived in the country for a long period of time. The use of expertise is not a retreat from objectivity. Judgment and informed opinion have always played a crucial role in human enterprises. Expert judgment can be incorporated into the structure of an investigation and can be made subject to some of the safeguards that are commonly used to assure objectivity in any scientific inquiry.

content.closest_integrated_transfers_stop_short_:
The dynamic constitutional-design framework is a strong near-direct precedent for using scenarios to test institutional alternatives. It says that design types correspond to forecasts or scenarios about democratic dynamics and that a baseline design emerges when a designer commits to those scenarios [closest_integrated_transfers_stop_short_of_the_full_bundle[0]] [5]. It compares constitutional alternatives through examples involving Hong Kong's electoral design and Nepal's modernization and identity challenges [closest_integrated_transfers_stop_short_of_the_full_bundle[0]] [5]. The framework is explicitly about constitutional design and evaluates designs over time rather than treating a constitution as static text [closest_integrated_transfers_stop_short_of_the_full_bundle[0]] [5] [closest_integrated_transfers_stop_short_of_the_full_bundle[0]] [5].

This framework contains C001's idea that difficult cases should reveal which interpretation or design performs better under different conditions. It does not, in the cited material, specify a panel's independent answers before deliberation or a preserved suite of resolved cases. Its "scenario" is primarily a forecast about political dynamics, whereas C001's case would be an operational test object with an answer and a later regression status.

The adjudication-learning study is closer on institutional recurrence, and Deliberative Polling is closer on sequencing. Democratic experimentalism is closer on iterative comparison and revision. But these are complementary near-direct precedents, not one integrated target-domain proposal. The search also found no authoritative source using the exact software term "regression testing" as a constitutional or deliberative-governance procedure. That negative result should be reported only as a corpus limitation, not converted into a claim of nonexistence.

### Component coverage matrix

| C001 component | Strongest precedent | Exact overlap | Material gap | Collision judgment |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| High-information cases distinguish competing values | Reflective equilibrium; Ashley's case comparison | Thought experiments expose strengths and weaknesses of principles; case comparison examines context, likeness, difference, and analogy [closest_integrated_transfers_stop_short_of_the_full_bundle[1]] [3] [closest_integrated_transfers_stop_short_of_the_full_bundle[2]] [4] | No located rule for selecting a "creative tail" or most information-rich cases | Direct root collision |
| Independent answers before deliberation | Deliberative Polling | Baseline questions precede discussion and are repeated afterward [closest_integrated_transfers_stop_short_of_the_full_bundle[3]] [1] | Baseline polling is not necessarily independent case classification or a formal anti-anchoring guarantee | Direct target-domain collision |
| Independent structured feedback and revision | Delphi | Individual questionnaires precede aggregated feedback, critique, and revision [closest_integrated_transfers_stop_short_of_the_full_bundle[4]] [16] | Classic Delphi is chiefly a forecasting and expert-elicitation method, not constitutional deliberation [closest_integrated_transfers_stop_short_of_the_full_bundle[5]] [7] | Strong source-domain analogue and governance transfer |
| Constitutional alternatives evaluated independently | Constitutional-design conjoint experiment | Respondents rate 26 randomized hypothetical constitutions [closest_integrated_transfers_stop_short_of_the_full_bundle[6]] [17] | No group deliberation, resolved-case archive, or future regression checks [closest_integrated_transfers_stop_short_of_the_full_bundle[6]] [17] | Direct target-domain partial collision |
| Resolved cases guide future interpretation | Constitutional precedent | Prior decisions receive deference and authority in later concrete disputes [closest_integrated_transfers_stop_short_of_the_full_bundle[7]] [6] | Precedent is authority, not a pass/fail regression oracle | Direct target-domain partial collision |
| Learning through repeated implementation and comparison | Democratic experimentalism; judicial learning | Rolling best practice, comparison, revised rights, and institutional change [closest_integrated_transfers_stop_short_of_the_full_bundle[8]] [18] [closest_integrated_transfers_stop_short_of_the_full_bundle[9]] [19] [closest_integrated_transfers_stop_short_of_the_full_bundle[9]] [19] | No explicit tail sample, pre-deliberation baseline, or regression-suite data structure | Near-direct integrated collision |
| All three stages as one operational architecture | No single source located in this corpus | The components can be assembled from target-domain precedents | Exact sequencing, case-selection policy, and persistent regression status remain unverified | Narrow residual only |

The matrix shows why a source-domain-only objection would be too weak. The first, second, fourth, and fifth rows have direct target-domain or near-target-domain support. The residual is correspondingly narrow: C001's claim can be original only as a disciplined synthesis that makes the links explicit and operational.
content.decision_standard_mechanism_collision_ve:
The candidate contains three separable operations: use cases to discriminate among interpretations, obtain judgments before interpersonal influence or collective convergence, and retain settled cases so later rules can be checked against them. I treat a **DIRECT COLLISION** as a single target-domain precedent that operationalizes all three operations as one repeatable architecture. I treat **ROOT COLLISION + NARROW RESIDUAL** as the result when each load-bearing operation is already established, but the exact sequencing, selection policy, or data structure remains unlocated.

This distinction matters because a source-domain analogy alone would be insufficient. Delphi began as a forecasting method, and software regression testing is an obvious analogy, but neither by itself establishes a constitutional or deliberative precedent. The relevant evidence is therefore weighted toward constitutional theory, legal adjudication, moral and political value interpretation, deliberative governance, and constitutional-design research. The constitutional-design experiment, constitutional precedent literature, dynamic-design framework, and judicial-learning study are target-domain or near-target-domain evidence; Delphi is used mainly to clarify the independence mechanism [decision_standard_mechanism_collision_versus_packaging_residual[0]] [7] [decision_standard_mechanism_collision_versus_packaging_residual[1]] [5] [decision_standard_mechanism_collision_versus_packaging_residual[2]] [19] [decision_standard_mechanism_collision_versus_packaging_residual[3]] [17].

The result is not that C001 has no creative content. It is that its creativity is more plausibly architectural and procedural than foundational. The candidate recombines established functions, and its residual must be stated at that narrower level.
content.disposition_residual_confidence_and_limi:
**Final disposition: ROOT COLLISION + NARROW RESIDUAL.** The candidate collides with established target-domain roots in three different senses. Reflective equilibrium and legal case comparison already use concrete cases to discriminate among values and principles [disposition_residual_confidence_and_limitations[0]] [3] [disposition_residual_confidence_and_limitations[1]] [4]. Deliberative Polling already measures views before and after collective discussion [disposition_residual_confidence_and_limitations[2]] [1]. Constitutional precedent and judicial-learning practices already preserve the consequences of earlier decisions and expose them to later disputes, evidence, and revision [disposition_residual_confidence_and_limitations[3]] [6] [disposition_residual_confidence_and_limitations[4]] [19] [disposition_residual_confidence_and_limitations[4]] [19].

The residual is narrower than the whole proposition. It consists of an explicit method for selecting high-information or adversarial-tail cases, a rule that records independent answers before deliberation on those cases, and a durable, versioned case suite whose resolved outputs are used as regression checks whenever a constitutional or value interpretation is changed. Neither constitutional precedent nor democratic experimentalism alone establishes that exact software-like operationalization. Precedent supplies durable authority; experimentalism supplies comparison and learning; reflective equilibrium supplies diagnostic cases; Deliberative Polling and Delphi supply pre-collective elicitation. C001's possible contribution is the integration and formal lifecycle, not the invention of those ingredients.

Confidence is **high** for the root-collision finding because multiple independent target-domain literatures cover the load-bearing functions. Confidence is **medium** for the narrow-residual finding because it is based on the sources located in this search rather than an exhaustive bibliographic review. The search was conducted primarily in English and emphasized accessible web-indexed scholarship, official method pages, law-review material, and extracted PDFs. It did not establish the absence of unpublished constitutional-convention protocols, non-English deliberative practices, proprietary governance systems, or differently named methods that might use an equivalent regression-suite architecture.

A further limitation is conceptual rather than bibliographic. "Independent" can mean private pre-discussion measurement, statistical independence, anonymous expert elicitation, or independence from social influence. Deliberative Polling clearly establishes the first meaning; Delphi more strongly addresses anonymity and independent response; neither automatically proves the others [disposition_residual_confidence_and_limitations[2]] [1] [disposition_residual_confidence_and_limitations[5]] [16]. Similarly, "regression test" can mean a binding precedent, an empirical benchmark, a recurring scenario, or a software-style expected-output check. The cited precedents establish the first three analogues, but not the fourth. Those distinctions support the narrow residual while preventing an overbroad originality claim.
content.executive_summary:
- **Interpretive Case Testing**: Reflective equilibrium uses thought experiments to expose the strengths and weaknesses of competing principles, while legal case comparison tests relevant likenesses and differences in concrete contexts [executive_summary[0]] [3] [executive_summary[1]] [4] -> treat the candidate's first component as an established target-domain method, not a new primitive.
- **Independent Baselines**: Deliberative Polling asks a representative sample the target questions before discussion and asks the same questions after deliberation [executive_summary[2]] [1]. The Delphi method separately elicits individual answers, supplies aggregated feedback, and permits revision [executive_summary[3]] [16] -> the pre-deliberation sequencing is established, although the two methods serve different legitimacy and expertise goals.
- **Constitutional Transfer**: A constitutional-design experiment had respondents rate **26** hypothetical constitutions with randomized rights and institutional attributes [executive_summary[4]] [17] -> independent scenario evaluation has already been transferred into constitutional-design research, but without group deliberation or durable case tests.
- **Retained Decisions**: Constitutional precedent gives prior decisions a role in later concrete disputes and grounds deference in constitutional structure, text, and historical context [executive_summary[5]] [6] -> retaining resolved cases for future interpretation is already a target-domain practice, although precedent is not the same as a regression oracle.
- **Adaptive Governance**: Democratic experimentalism uses local variation, comparison, rolling best-practice requirements, and revision based on which arrangements perform better [executive_summary[6]] [18]. Judicial institutional-learning research likewise links adjudication, deliberation, experimentation, and institutional change [executive_summary[7]] [19] -> the learning loop surrounding C001 has credible target-domain precedents.
- **Closest Concrete Transfer**: In *United States v. Fallbrook Public Utilities District*, a water-rights action involving **6,000 defendants** used stipulated facts and court memoranda as default conditions while preserving opportunities to contradict them [executive_summary[7]] [19] -> concrete disputes, provisional resolutions, later challenge, and institutional learning can coexist in a governance process.
- **Narrow Residual**: I did not locate one credible target-domain source that explicitly combines deliberate high-information or tail-case selection, independent pre-deliberation answers, and a versioned repository of resolved cases used as pass/fail regression tests. This is a search result, not proof that no such source exists -> any originality claim should be limited to that exact coordination and operationalization.
- **Final Disposition**: **ROOT COLLISION + NARROW RESIDUAL**. Confidence is high that the three load-bearing roots already exist in the target domain or its closest governance transfers, and medium that no single integrated precedent was found in the searched corpus -> do not claim mechanism-level originality; claim only possible novelty in the explicit synthesis, selection rule, and regression-suite implementation.
content.independent_answers_before_deliberation_:
The clearest target-domain institutional precedent is **Deliberative Polling**. The official Stanford description says that a random, representative sample is first polled on the targeted issues, then invited to discuss them over a weekend, and then asked the original questions again after deliberation [independent_answers_before_deliberation_are_established_in_two_forms[0]] [1]. This directly contains the sequence "answer first, deliberate second, answer again." It also allows researchers to observe whether and how opinions change after exposure to information and discussion.

The method is not identical to C001. Its baseline survey is a measurement and accountability device, not necessarily a formal independence assumption in the Condorcet sense. It typically asks citizens about a public issue rather than asking them to classify a curated set of edge cases. The official page nevertheless records applications to concrete issues: South Korean citizens deliberated in **August 2011** about the conditions, timing, and consequences of unification; a Polish process in **November 2009** addressed the future of the Bulgarska Street Stadium; and a European Union sample deliberated about European Parliament elections in **June 2009** [independent_answers_before_deliberation_are_established_in_two_forms[0]] [1]. These are public-governance precedents for sequencing individual measurement and collective deliberation.

The **Delphi method** supplies a stronger independence mechanism but comes from a source-domain methodology. RAND describes sequential individual interrogations, normally questionnaires, interspersed with information and opinion feedback derived from a computed consensus [independent_answers_before_deliberation_are_established_in_two_forms[1]] [16]. Respondents first record individual estimates, receive medians, interquartile ranges, reasons, and counterarguments, and then reconsider or revise their answers [independent_answers_before_deliberation_are_established_in_two_forms[1]] [16]. Direct committee debate is eliminated in the procedure described by the original research [independent_answers_before_deliberation_are_established_in_two_forms[1]] [16]. RAND's current account describes Delphi as having originated in the 1950s and later being applied to health care, education, management, and environmental science [independent_answers_before_deliberation_are_established_in_two_forms[2]] [7].

### Case study: constitutional-design experiments isolate judgments before discussion

The constitutional-design experiment is the closest direct transfer of independent scenario evaluation into the target domain. Respondents evaluated **26** hypothetical constitutions whose rights and institutional attributes were randomly assigned, including freedoms, social rights, federalism, constitutional courts, and military constraints [independent_answers_before_deliberation_are_established_in_two_forms[3]] [17] [independent_answers_before_deliberation_are_established_in_two_forms[3]] [17]. Attribute ordering was also randomized to reduce order effects [independent_answers_before_deliberation_are_established_in_two_forms[3]] [17].

This case establishes that constitutional preferences can be elicited through controlled exposure to multiple hypothetical constitutional profiles rather than only through a single abstract question. The study reports average marginal component effects, not a deliberative process or a persistent case library [independent_answers_before_deliberation_are_established_in_two_forms[3]] [17]. It therefore collides with C001's independent evaluation of concrete constitutional alternatives, but not with the later group-deliberation and regression-test stages. The important residual is not "use scenarios in constitutional design"; that is already documented. It is the explicit pipeline from scenario selection to independent judgments to durable future tests.
content.precedent_experimentalism_and_institutio:
Constitutional precedent is the strongest target-domain analogue for preserving resolved cases. Kozel's constitutional-structure account states that the Constitution does not expressly discuss precedent, but that several constitutional features support deference to prior decisions; taken together, structure, text, and historical context support that inference [precedent_experimentalism_and_institutional_learning_preserve_the_past[0]] [6]. The account expressly connects precedent to concrete disputes and explains why the Supreme Court may legitimately reaffirm constitutional precedents even when they are flawed [precedent_experimentalism_and_institutional_learning_preserve_the_past[0]] [6].

Precedent therefore contains C001's persistence function: an earlier concrete decision remains available as an authoritative input to later interpretation. It also contains a distinction operation, because later cases must be related to, followed, limited, or distinguished from earlier decisions. The difference is normative and institutional. A legal precedent is not normally a pass/fail test of a proposed constitutional interpretation; it is an authority whose force depends on doctrine, institutional role, and reasons.

**Democratic experimentalism** supplies a different, more adaptive near-precedent. Dorf and Sabel describe arrangements in which jurisdictions or agencies retain differing definitions while experimentation shows which regime produces a superior standard, with comparison and search rather than a single central limit establishing a rolling best-practice requirement [precedent_experimentalism_and_institutional_learning_preserve_the_past[1]] [18]. The same account distinguishes short-run problem-solving from long-run learning [precedent_experimentalism_and_institutional_learning_preserve_the_past[1]] [18]. This is close to regression testing in function: past implementations generate comparative evidence that constrains later standards. It is not regression testing in the software sense because the source does not specify a fixed suite of edge cases, an immutable expected output, or an explicit pass/fail check.

### Case study: judicial learning converts failed rules into revised rights

The judicial-learning research links courts to experimentation, deliberation, and institutional change in complex resource problems [precedent_experimentalism_and_institutional_learning_preserve_the_past[2]] [19]. Its groundwater example describes a failure of fixed safe-yield determinations: basin conditions proved more favorable than estimated, and fixed rights prevented pumpers from using sustainable capacity [precedent_experimentalism_and_institutional_learning_preserve_the_past[2]] [19]. A later fisheries example moved from fixed quantitative rights to proportionate rights that fluctuated with newly collected and assessed resource information [precedent_experimentalism_and_institutional_learning_preserve_the_past[2]] [19].

The case study is a near-direct transfer into governance because adjudication does not merely decide an isolated dispute. It produces rules, exposes those rules to later facts and litigation, and can revise them when the information environment changes. That is the same observation-to-update direction as a regression loop. The missing pieces are exactly the ones C001 should not overstate as already established: no explicit high-information tail-sampling rule, no stated independent-answer protocol before deliberation, and no named regression-test suite [precedent_experimentalism_and_institutional_learning_preserve_the_past[2]] [19] [precedent_experimentalism_and_institutional_learning_preserve_the_past[2]] [19].
content.reflective_equilibrium_and_case_comparis:
The strongest direct precedent for the first component is the philosophical method of **reflective equilibrium**. The method brings judgments and principles into agreement after considering a wide range of considerations [reflective_equilibrium_and_case_comparison_already_test_values[0]] [3]. It explicitly treats thought experiments as arguments, including examples such as utilitarian sheriffs, utility monsters, experience machines, trolley problems, and repugnant conclusions; these cases are used to show the strengths and weaknesses of principles under consideration [reflective_equilibrium_and_case_comparison_already_test_values[0]] [3]. Initial judgments are revisable, and the method does not treat the starting point as fixed [reflective_equilibrium_and_case_comparison_already_test_values[0]] [3].

That is a close structural match for using carefully chosen concrete cases to distinguish plausible interpretations of a constitutional value. The case need not be statistically representative. Its function is diagnostic: it places a principle under pressure, makes a latent implication visible, or exposes a conflict between a general rule and a considered judgment. C001's phrase "high-information concrete cases" may therefore be a new label or selection emphasis, but the underlying interpretive move is already central to a target-domain theory of moral and political reasoning.

Kevin Ashley's primary account of case-based legal reasoning makes the overlap more operational. It describes case comparison as a way to address competing principles and emphasizes that practical ethics and policy creation require attention to particular contexts and the consequences of particular features [reflective_equilibrium_and_case_comparison_already_test_values[1]] [4]. It also identifies a structured analysis of analogy: determine what is known, unclear, and presumed; examine relevant likenesses and differences; and inspect the potentially misleading sources of an analogy's appeal [reflective_equilibrium_and_case_comparison_already_test_values[1]] [4]. This is not merely storytelling about examples. It is a procedure for deciding which facts should change the interpretation or application of a general principle.

### Case study: Fallbrook turns concrete disputes into revisable institutional knowledge

The judicial-learning study of *United States v. Fallbrook Public Utilities District* provides a governance case rather than a purely philosophical example. The water-rights action involved **6,000 defendants**; extensive discovery and a four-day pretrial conference generated stipulated facts and court memoranda governing legal issues [reflective_equilibrium_and_case_comparison_already_test_values[2]] [19]. The agreed facts became default conditions unless displaced, while parties retained opportunities to cross-examine or present contradictory evidence [reflective_equilibrium_and_case_comparison_already_test_values[2]] [19].

The decision architecture reveals both the collision and the residual. A concrete dispute supplied information, a provisional resolution made that information administrable, and later contradiction remained possible. The study also describes repeated litigation as creating opportunities to overturn inefficient rules and reports movement from fixed quantitative rights toward proportionate rights when new resource information became available [reflective_equilibrium_and_case_comparison_already_test_values[2]] [19] [reflective_equilibrium_and_case_comparison_already_test_values[2]] [19]. What it does not provide is a pre-deliberation independent-answer stage or an explicit regression-test repository. C001's case-selection and persistence language therefore adds a specific control layer to an already familiar case-learning pattern.
content.synthesis:
The precedents differ along mechanism, scope, authority, and time horizon. The comparison is more informative than asking whether any one source uses the same label.

| Framework or practice | Primary unit | How it handles disagreement | What persists | Time horizon and trade-off |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Reflective equilibrium | Judgments, principles, and thought experiments | Revises judgments and principles until they fit a considered set of reasons [synthesis[0]] [3] | A justified or coherent set of principles, not a fixed case suite | Philosophical and iterative; high diagnostic flexibility but weak institutional persistence |
| Deliberative Polling | Representative citizens and public issues | Baseline survey, information, small-group discussion, and repeat survey [synthesis[1]] [1] | Before/after measurements and public findings | Event-level or longitudinal; strong legitimacy and measurement, but not a formal regression oracle |
| Delphi | Experts or stakeholders and structured questions | Anonymous individual answers, aggregate feedback, counterarguments, and revision [synthesis[2]] [7] [synthesis[3]] [16] | Group response and reasons across rounds | Iterative and expertise-oriented; protects against direct group pressure, but can sacrifice ordinary-citizen legitimacy |
| Constitutional precedent | Judicial decisions and later concrete disputes | Follow, distinguish, limit, reaffirm, or overrule earlier decisions [synthesis[4]] [6] | Authoritative holdings and reasons | Long institutional horizon; stability and continuity can preserve flawed rules |
| Democratic experimentalism | Local institutional arrangements and comparative performance | Variation, peer comparison, rolling standards, and revision [synthesis[5]] [18] | Benchmarks, practices, and lessons from implementation | Ongoing and adaptive; supports learning but may be difficult to standardize |
| C001 residual | Curated high-information constitutional/value cases | Independent pre-deliberation answers followed by collective interpretation | A versioned, resolved case suite used as future regression checks | Recurring lifecycle; gains auditability but must solve case-selection bias and authority questions |

Three tensions define the residual. First, reflective equilibrium treats initial judgments as revisable, while precedent values continuity and may reaffirm flawed decisions [synthesis[0]] [3] [synthesis[4]] [6]. C001 would need a governance rule for when a regression case remains a binding expectation and when new deliberation may legitimately revise it.

Second, independence and deliberation pull in opposite directions. Delphi eliminates direct committee debate in favor of structured feedback [synthesis[3]] [16], whereas Deliberative Polling deliberately brings people together after a baseline measurement [synthesis[1]] [1]. C001's distinctive design question is not whether to choose one or the other, but whether the pre-deliberation answers are preserved as an auditable baseline while the later deliberation is allowed to change the answer.

Third, experimentalist governance learns from variation, while a regression suite normally treats a prior output as a stable expected result. The judicial-learning cases show why governance rules sometimes must change when new information arrives [synthesis[6]] [19]. Therefore, the residual should not promise automatic preservation of every old answer as permanently correct. A defensible C001 implementation would preserve the case, its prior resolution, the reasons for that resolution, and the conditions under which the resolution may be reopened. That is a narrower and more credible originality claim than saying that cases, independent judgment, or institutional learning are themselves new.
